title: AWS Ships Continuum for Code Vulnerabilities
gist: AWS made Continuum for code vulnerabilities GA in two US regions, an agentic service that validates findings by running exploits in a sandbox and proposes patches, priced per line of code plus a per-finding inference fee that reaches roughly $20 per validated finding at scale. AWS plans to grant autonomous fixing for classes of fixes, but unlike Google's CodeMender it does not verify that patches preserve behavior, and product boundaries with AWS Security Agent remain muddled.

insights.claim: AWS made Continuum for code vulnerabilities generally available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) four months after announcing it in gated preview.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: AWS is entering the application security market directly with an agentic product, pressuring standalone AppSec vendors.
insights.locator: AWS recently made Continuum for code

insights.claim: AWS executives Swami Sivasubramanian and Christopher Rae frame the code-security problem as alert volume rather than detection, saying organizations with large application estates see thousands of scanner findings a day, most of which are noise.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The value in AppSec is shifting from finding vulnerabilities to triaging and fixing them, threatening scanner-only vendors.
insights.quote: most becomes noise that doesn't matter in your environment.
insights.locator: Swami Sivasubramanian, VP of Agentic AI

insights.claim: Continuum builds a context graph from connected repositories and the AWS environment, confirms reachability by running exploits in an isolated sandbox with proof-of-concept code, and outputs an attack path and blast radius assessment rather than a risk score alone, delivering fixes as patches or pull requests.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Exploit-proven prioritization is becoming the new competitive bar for vulnerability management tools.
insights.quote: a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone.
insights.locator: The validation step is the answer

insights.claim: A sandbox proof shows code is exploitable but not that the path exists in a customer's environment, and AWS documents nothing about what happens to findings Continuum cannot prove, risking them becoming an ignored 'safe pile'.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Unproven findings are a blind spot that could create false assurance and liability for adopters.
insights.quote: the findings it cannot prove still need somewhere to go, or they quietly become the safe pile.
insights.locator: A proof in an isolated sandbox

insights.claim: Continuum pricing has a context fee per million lines of code protected per month, starting at $200 and tiering down to $100 above ten billion lines, plus an inference fee of $10 per Continuum inference unit consumed as findings are worked.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Usage-based pricing tied to findings shows how hyperscalers will monetize agentic AI security workloads.

insights.claim: In AWS's worked examples, one million lines with 100 vulnerabilities costs $1,200, while 100 million lines with 10,000 vulnerabilities at two units each costs $218,200, of which $200,000 is inference, roughly $20 per validated finding.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Inference dominates cost at scale, so AWS revenue grows with vulnerability volume, aligning incentives oddly with the noise problem it claims to solve.
insights.quote: The thousands of daily findings both executives describe, and the per-finding fee, measure the same workload from opposite ends.

insights.claim: AWS penetration testing remains separately priced at $50 per task-hour, and threat modeling, announced in preview in June, has no published pricing; only the code vulnerabilities capability reached GA.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: AWS is building an agentic security suite with metered per-task pricing across multiple products.

insights.claim: Every Continuum remediation currently requires human approval before shipping, but AWS plans to let it apply classes of fixes autonomously once confidence criteria such as test coverage and historical success rate are met.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Autonomous code remediation would sharply expand the addressable spend for agentic dev tools and reduce security headcount needs.
insights.quote: every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships,
insights.locator: Where the announcement points is autonomy

insights.claim: Former AWS principal Jorg Huser warned that an overloaded review queue could itself become the reason to grant AI fixers more autonomy, arguing autonomous merge should require evidence that fixes remove the vulnerability and preserve behavior.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Governance pressure on autonomous fixing could slow adoption or create incident risk for early adopters.
insights.quote: An overloaded review queue can otherwise become the reason to grant more autonomy.
insights.locator: Jorg Huser, a CTO and former

insights.claim: Google's CodeMender also proves exploitability by running an exploit but additionally validates each patch with an LLM-as-a-judge framework testing program equivalence, a step AWS's own console caveat concedes Continuum does not perform.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Google holds a technical edge on patch verification in the AI code-security race.
insights.quote: without altering the application's intended behavior.

insights.claim: AWS product boundaries remain confusing: the Continuum guide covers code vulnerabilities while penetration testing and threat modeling sit in a separately titled AWS Security Agent User Guide, echoing Yan Cui's July complaint of two product names for the same capabilities.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Product sprawl may slow AWS adoption and leave room for focused competitors.
insights.quote: we have the same capabilities, two product names, and no clarity on which one you should use,
